That is simply not the case. In space there is insufficient density of the medium for a mechanical wave to propagate. That's why there's no sound in space. Any explosion that occurs can only do so within the confines of it's own explosive material, adjacent material, or material generated by the explosion, that's basic physics.

In the case of a nuke, the fissile material will be detonated and expand into the resulting near-field (the area where gasses and material inherent to the explosive itself will "instantaneously" expand to). The energy it gives off will be confined to the electromagnetic, radioactive, and visible light, while the heat will be mostly insulated and overpressure will simply dissipate into the vacuum of space. It will not impart any sufficient momentum to the asteroid.

In order for the nuke to even begin to do something, it would have to impact the inbound asteroid in order to transfer any effective amount of energy to it. At that point it becomes a matter of structural dynamics as to whether or not it will impart sufficient energy to fracture the asteroid.

Even NASA's assertion that a near-field detonation would vaporize the surface of the asteroid creating sufficient dust cast-off to redirect the asteroid is spurious at best. The ablative affect would be highly dependent on the asteroids material composition and since there have never been experiments performed, could range from nothing to anything. The assertion that that dust ablated by vaporization could provide sufficient thrust to push a massive object away is also overly optimistic, as Newtonian mechanics illustrates. Only if by chance the asteroid was caught far enough away, and only in the best of projections, could the method have any hope of being sufficient to deflect an asteroid into a safe trajectory.
